input: Asynchronous learning environments (ALEs) have become a critical complement and extension to traditional synchronous learning (e.g., live lectures and real-time tutoring). By removing time and location constraints, ALEs enhance flexibility and inclusivity, supporting more equitable access to educational resources and opportunities [#CITE#]. However, providing timely and effective instructional support remains one of the biggest challenges for ALE adoption. Their self-paced, decentralized nature makes it difficult for instructors to track progress and manage interactions, often leading to delayed feedback that can reduce student motivation, engagement, and learning effectiveness [#CITE#]. Virtual Teaching Assistants (VTAs) offer a promising approach to address this challenge by providing scalable, timely, and personalized support, helping reduce instructor workload in ALEs [#CITE#]. They are often powered by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approaches to respond quickly to student questions [#CITE#]. While earlier systems focused on routine and syllabus-based questions [#CITE#], recent VTAs powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) can tackle more complex academic queries [#CITE#]. Although these advancements highlight the growing capabilities of VTAs, the pedagogical effectiveness of their generated content still lacks a systematic and scalable evaluation framework, which is a critical issue. Early approaches often rely on manual qualitative analyses [#CITE#] or general-purpose language metrics [#CITE#] to assess similarity to human responses. Nevertheless, these metrics are not designed to assess teaching quality and often lack generalizability across different educational contexts. To bridge this gap, we propose a pedagogical teaching assistant evaluation framework grounded in learning science, focusing on VTAs in asynchronous online forums, one of the most common deployment contexts in ALEs. The framework has two components: a five-level pedagogical skill model with progressively increasing ``instructional difficulty'': (1) Clarify Misunderstandings and Confusions, (2) Deepen Disciplinary Understanding, (3) Foster Higher-Order Thinking, (4) Enhance Metacognitive Awareness, and (5) Foster Collaborative Knowledge Construction developed by linking core cognitive mechanisms to pedagogical goals, and an evaluation rubric that operationalizes this model by specifying observable instructional behaviors at each level. When establishing the usability and reliability of our rubric, we utilize a set of simulated VTA responses on student discussion forum posts collected through an IRB-approved procedure. Note that Level 5 of our framework is currently unattainable for most VTAs, as their responses are typically limited to a single forum post and any retrieved content, excluding broader context from other posts in the discussion. However, asynchronous online forums are inherently community-driven spaces, and achieving collaborative knowledge construction requires access to broader, forum-level context. To simulate VTAs with broader forum-level post access for Level 5 evaluations, we use RAG to create responses informed by similar peer posts. Expert annotators apply our rubrics to these simulated responses. We then leverage these annotations to build automatic classifiers using LLMs. [#CITE#] reports negative correlations between LLM and expert annotations in tutor pedagogical assessment, indicating that LLMs may be unreliable evaluators. Their study uses a single, unoptimized prompt without fine-tuning, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation. We extend this line of inquiry to the VTA pedagogical evaluation context by systematically exploring whether prompt optimization and fine-tuning can improve alignment between LLM-based evaluators and expert pedagogical judgments. Our expert annotation results indicate that including peer forum posts reduces pedagogical capability in Levels 1-4 within our specific simulated VTA environment. Furthermore, while our automated classifiers perform reliably on lower-level, in-distribution examples, they struggle at higher pedagogical levels and exhibit limited generalization, even for Level 1. input: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have achieved many successes in challenging tasks, including magnetic plasma control [#CITE#], automobile racing[#CITE#], and robotics[#CITE#]. However, applying existing RL algorithms to every new task in a tabula rasa manner often results in low sample efficiency that limits RL's broader applicability [#CITE#]. Unsupervised skill discovery holds the promise of improving the sample efficiency of Reinforcement Learning, by learning a set of reusable skills through reward-free interaction with the environment that can be later recombined to tackle multiple downstream tasks more efficiently. In practice, prior unsupervised RL skills are represented as a policy that conditions on a skill variable to generate diverse behaviors, and have led to successful and efficient learning of downstream tasks when combined with skill fine-tuning or hierarchical RL skill selection[#CITE#]. Despite prior successes, a common limitation of the skills learned by existing unsupervised RL methods is that they are entangled: any change in the skill variable causes the agent to induce changes in multiple dimensions of the state space simultaneously. Learning to use and recombine these entangled skills can be extremely hard for an agent trying to solve downstream tasks, especially in complex domains like multi-agent systems or household humanoid robots, where the agent needs to concurrently change multiple independent dimensions of the state to complete the task. For example, consider an agent learning to operate a car: if a single skill variable simultaneously changes the speed, steering, and headlights of the car, it will be extremely challenging for the agent to learn how to turn on/off the headlights while keeping the car at the right speed and direction. In contrast, humans naturally have the ability to concurrently and independently adjust the car's acceleration, steering, and headlights based on the car's current speed, surroundings, and lighting conditions. In other words, humans naturally obtain disentangled skill components where each component only affects one or few state variables, and can easily recombine these skill components into compositional skills [#CITE#] to control multiple factors simultaneously. In this work, we aim to create such a mechanism for artificial agents to learn disentangled skills that facilitate solving downstream tasks. We introduce (), a novel method for unsupervised discovery of disentangled skills. A key insight of is to take advantage of state factorization that is naturally available in unsupervised RL environments[#CITE#] (e.g. speed, direction, and lighting conditions of the car in the driving example; the state of different objects in a household environment). These factored state spaces provide a natural inductive bias we leverage for disentanglement: decomposes skills into disentangled components, and encourages each skill component to affect only one state factor while discouraging it from affecting any other factors. To that end, designs a novel intrinsic reward for unsupervised skill learning based on mutual information (MI) between disentangled skills and state factors: the learning agent receives high rewards for 1) increasing the MI between a state factor and the skill component assigned to change it, and 2) for decreasing the MI between that skill component and all other state factors. introduces a set of technical innovations to tractably and efficiently optimize the proposed mutual information objective. Once the skills are learned, they can be used as the low-level policy in a hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) setting to tackle downstream tasks. Compared to using entangled skills, a key benefit of using the disentangled skills is that they guarantee more efficient exploration during downstream task learning and therefore often lead to significantly better performance. Furthermore, the structured skill space of opens up additional possibilities to inject domain knowledge into the learning process to further improve the efficiency of both skill learning and downstream task learning. is easy to implement and can be integrated into any MI-based unsupervised skill discovery approach. In our experiments, we integrate with DIAYN[#CITE#] and evaluate the performance on four domains: a 2D agent navigation domain, a DMC walker domain, a large-scale multi-agent particle domain, and a 3D realistic simulated robotics domain. Our experiments indicate that can indeed learn disentangled skills, and significantly outperforms other Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning methods on solving complex downstream tasks with HRL.
